articles.title: Debt Mutual Funds: What investors should know before investing
articles.summary: Debt mutual funds saw a net outflow of Rs 1.8 lakh crore in September, the highest monthly withdrawal in the first half of FY27. Despite this, they remain an important investment avenue for investors looking to park surplus money, manage short-term goals and diversify their portfolios. A look at how debt funds work and what investors should know before investing.WHAT ARE DEBT MUTUAL FUNDS?Debt mutual funds invest in fixed-income instruments such as government securities, treasury bills, corporate bonds, commercial paper and certificates of deposit. They aim to provide relatively stable returns while taking lower risk than equity funds. Debt funds generate returns in two ways. The first is through the interest earned on the bonds and other securities held in the portfolio. The second comes from changes in bond prices. When bond prices rise, fund managers can book gains by selling these securities.HOW SHOULD INVESTORS CHOOSE A DEBT FUND? The choice depends on the investment horizon, liquidity needs and ability to tolerate fluctuations in returns. Investors looking to park money for a few days or months may consider overnight or liquid funds. Those with a horizon of six months to two years may look at ultra-short duration, low duration or money-market funds. For investment horizons of three years or more, categories such as short-duration funds, corporate bond funds and banking & PSU debt funds may be suitable. Gilt funds and long-duration funds are generally more appropriate for investors who understand interest-rate cycles.Read more: Smallcap mutual fund inflows drop 29% MoM to Rs 6,407 crore in October. Should investors be cautious or continue investing?WHY DID DEBT FUNDS WITNESS LARGE OUTFLOWS IN SEPTEMBER? The large outflows were largely driven by liquidity requirements rather than a change in investor appetite for debt funds. These schemes are widely used by companies and institutional investors to park surplus cash for short periods. September is also a quarter-end month when companies usually withdraw money to meet working capital requirements, advance tax payments and other financial obligations.Read more: Debt mutual funds see sharp recovery in October as quarter-end outflows reverseARE DEBT FUNDS RISK-FREE? While debt funds are generally less volatile than equity funds, they are not risk-free. One key risk is interest-rate risk. When interest rates rise, bond prices fall, which can affect the value of a fund’s portfolio. The second is credit risk, which arises when a company or other issuer fails to repay its debt or interest on time. Funds investing in lower-rated corporate bonds generally carry higher credit risk.HOW DO INTEREST RATES AFFECT DEBT FUND RETURNS? Interest rates and bond prices move in opposite directions. When interest rates fall, existing bonds offering higher interest become more attractive to investors. As demand for these bonds rises, their prices generally move up. This, in turn, tends to benefit debt funds. When interest rates rise, bond prices usually decline, which can weigh on returns. Long-duration funds are usually more affected by interest-rate changes, while liquid and overnight funds tend to see smaller fluctuations.

articles.summary: CoreWeave shares surged more than 26% on Wednesday, fuelling a rally in battered AI cloud stocks after heavy infrastructure spending delivered strong revenue growth and the company signalled a retreat from the borrowing spree that had raised fears of an artificial intelligence bubble, Reuters reported.CoreWeave shares were trading at $61.61, up $12.88 or 26.43% over the previous close.The results also helped lift Nvidia, a major CoreWeave backer, by 2%. Nvidia had fallen sharply over the previous two sessions amid uncertainty surrounding CEO Jensen Huang following reports about his relationship with a Chinese businesswoman alleged to have ties to Beijing’s intelligence apparatus.Shares of other so-called neocloud companies, including Nebius and Iren, also rallied after weeks of pressure. Investors have worried that their debt-funded data-centre expansion could backfire if demand for AI computing weakens.For live updates on US Markets, click here“CoreWeave’s earnings directly addressed the fear that’s driven this whole selloff,” said Dan Sheehan, director of portfolio management at Telos Wealth Advisors, according to Reuters. “The neocloud that became the poster child for AI financing worries took real weight off the fear that had been the heart of the selloff.”Democrats’ sweep of last week’s US midterm elections had further unsettled the industry. Several victorious candidates campaigned for stricter regulation and moratoriums on new data-centre construction, including in Texas, a key market for the sector.CoreWeave CEO Michael Intrator told Reuters on Tuesday that increased regulatory scrutiny could slow data-centre development across the industry. However, he did not expect it to significantly affect the company’s expansion plans or raise costs.Intrator said CoreWeave’s planned capacity additions over the next year would remain unaffected.Also Read: Is AI wheel broken? Julius Baer flags 3 variables shaping AI investments ahead of Anthropic IPOThe company also said it would avoid unsecured debt markets following a recent surge in borrowing costs. Cash flow from existing contracts would cover repayments on both current and future debt, it added—a financing plan analysts described as credible.“CoreWeave delivered about the best quarter we could have asked for. Stats were good-to-great, funding concerns were addressed and the strategic moves make sense,” Bernstein analysts led by Madison Rezaei said in a client note.However, they warned that CoreWeave “will be among the first and hardest hit” once the shortage of AI computing capacity eases.The risks of mistiming AI investments were evident on Tuesday when SoftBank recorded a $3.7 billion write-down on non-refundable payments for equipment intended to power its US data centres. The charge contributed to a second-quarter net loss of $7 billion, the company’s first in nearly two years.Uncertainty surrounding Huang has also weighed on the AI sector. The controversy intensified on Tuesday after reports alleged that his relationship helped facilitate billions of dollars in Nvidia chip shipments to China.Republican US Senator Kevin Cramer, a member of the Senate Banking Committee, called on Huang to step down as Nvidia CEO.For now, CoreWeave’s results have given AI infrastructure investors some relief. Nebius, Iren, Oracle and Applied Digital climbed between 6% and 14%.With the exception of Nebius, the stocks had fallen between 32% and 48% this year through Tuesday. Nebius, by contrast, had gained 60%.Together, the companies—including CoreWeave—were on track to add about $36 billion in market value if the gains held. Nvidia alone was positioned to gain nearly $100 billion.Nebius is scheduled to report its results before Thursday’s opening bell.(Disclaimer: This article is based on inputs from agencies. articles.title: Nvidia rebounds after $480 billion wipeout
articles.summary: Nvidia stock (NVDA) surged nearly 4% in premarket trading on Wednesday, November 11, as investors bought the dip after a two-day sell-off that wiped roughly $480 billion from the chipmaker's market value. Shares rose to $175.45 at 6:49 a.m. ET, up 3.88%, after closing Tuesday at $168.89, down $9.78, or 5.47%.The rebound came alongside gains in US stock futures, with Nasdaq 100 futures rising 1.67%, S&P 500 futures gaining 0.74% and Dow futures edging up 0.03%.Investors are returning to AI stocks even as Nvidia faces an investigation involving CEO Jensen Huang, just six days before its November 17 earnings report.Why is Nvidia stock rising today after a $480 billion market value crash?Nvidia's rebound comes after two difficult trading sessions. Shares fell 4.3% on Monday and another 5.47% on Tuesday as investors reacted to reports about Huang's relationship with a woman suspected by US intelligence of having links to Chinese intelligence.The stock closed Monday at $178.67 before falling to $168.89 on Tuesday. Wednesday's premarket recovery has helped Nvidia regain part of those losses, although shares remain below their level before the controversy intensified.The recovery is also part of a broader rally in AI stocks. CoreWeave shares gained more than 10% in premarket trading after its quarterly results helped ease concerns about AI infrastructure spending. Micron and Marvell also rose nearly 7%.Nvidia faces Jensen Huang investigation as board hires outside law firmNvidia confirmed on Tuesday that its independent directors had hired Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz to investigate whether company secrets or US national security had been compromised.The investigation will be led by former acting US Attorney Joon H. Kim.The company had already announced an independent review on Sunday. Nvidia's board said it had no reason to believe that company secrets or national security had been compromised. It also expressed confidence in Huang and his leadership team.The allegations remain unproven, and China has denied claims of an espionage operation.Huang returned to Nvidia's office on Monday and continued holding meetings on Tuesday, according to CNBC. His return comes as investors assess whether the controversy could affect Nvidia's operations or leadership.Bank of America warns Nvidia could face three different outcomesBank of America outlined three possible scenarios for Nvidia in a research note on Tuesday.The first involves a contained investigation with no major disruption to leadership. Under this outcome, investor attention could return to Nvidia's earnings and AI chip demand.The second involves prolonged uncertainty that puts pressure on the company's valuation ahead of its quarterly results.The third carries greater financial risks. Bank of America analyst Vivek Arya warned that adverse findings, leadership changes or tighter restrictions could require investors to reassess Nvidia's earnings outlook.Morgan Stanley removes Nvidia stock from top picks after 25% declineMorgan Stanley removed Nvidia from its top stock picks on Wednesday after shares dropped more than 25% since the bank added the company to its list on October 2.The bank's analysts said Huang's leadership remains crucial to Nvidia's strategic direction.The decision adds to concerns about how much Nvidia's market valuation depends on its chief executive.Zacks Chief Equity Strategist John Blank also warned that investors were concerned about possible additional US restrictions and further developments in the investigation.Speaking to CNBC, Blank said the situation was negative for Nvidia, Huang and the broader AI trade.Nvidia earnings on November 17: Can NVDA stock sustain its recovery?Nvidia's next quarterly earnings report is scheduled for November 17, giving investors another major event to watch.The market will focus on revenue growth, AI chip demand, profit margins and the company's guidance for the coming quarter.

I am deeply sorry,” the 63-year-old Taiwanese-born executive said.Also read | Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang faces leadership questions as Republican senator calls for his resignationMichael Burry takes U-turn on Nvidia?Notably, Michael Burry had been shorting Nvidia shares until September, when he announced that he is exiting some of the put options. The American investor later exited some of the put options, triggering some optimism, but Burry clarified that it was not his intention.Burry said he sold his December 2026 puts on both Nvidia and Palantir entirely to avoid rapid time-based decay. He added that he did not replace or roll the positions, saying he is "pulling back on exposures across the portfolio." Michael Burry's AI warningsThe American investor who famously correctly predicted the 2008 US housing crisis has been sounding the alarm since the beginning of the year over a prospective big market crash when the AI frenzy fizzles out. Earlier this year, Burry said he continues to believe that the market is close to a major top, warning of a similar crash to that of 1987 when Dow Jones recorded a historic 23% plunge, which led to the introduction of regulatory circuit breakers. However, the market investor noted that the S&P 500 making new highs likely will bring new money into the market.He wrote in a Substack post that he sees many indicators, both technical and fundamental, lining up for the same conclusion as the Dotcom crash. "1999 went where no market had gone before, and I would say so can this one...It is already there on several indicators," he said, arguing that massive venture capital flows, rising AI debt issuance, and extreme market optimism are creating conditions where valuations may detach from economic reality.Also read | Anthropic retracts details of $69 billion IPO filing sent to bankers. articles.title: China builds inside Europe's walls
articles.summary: Sofia: China doesn't need to clear Europe's trade barriers. It can build inside them.Chinese companies are establishing production and supplier networks across Central and Eastern Europe, which could enable them to gain more control over the technologies and inputs that European manufacturing needs.China is increasingly challenging the European Union in the advanced manufacturing sectors that helped the EU weather the first China shock, which reshaped global manufacturing in the 2000s. Chinese firms are competing with the EU in chemicals, machinery, advanced equipment and autos - and increasingly coming out on top on both price and quality.The EU trade deficit with China has nearly quadrupled over the past decade, from around €100 billion in 2014 to over €370 billion in 2025, or roughly €1 billion a day, according to Eurostat data.France and Germany are seeking to push back with stronger trade defences, but import curbs will achieve little if Chinese investment, ownership and control of critical technologies recreates the same vulnerabilities inside the single market.LOOKING EASTCentral and Eastern Europe appear to be key to China's growth strategy in Europe.While the EU's trade deficit with China has hovered around 2% of EU gross domestic product (GDP) since 2014, it has risen sharply in parts of CEE. For example, Slovenia's goods deficit with China rose from 2.5% to 16% over that period. Meanwhile, Poland's goods deficit surged from €8.9 billion to €34.3 billion, equivalent to about 5.2% of GDP. The Czech Republic's deficit nearly quadrupled to €22 billion, or roughly 8% of GDP, and Hungary's tripled to €10.4 billion, or about 6% of GDP.Investment and corporate ties deepened that exposure. In 2025, Chinese foreign direct investment (FDI) flows into the EU approached €16.8 billion, and the cumulative value of Chinese investment in the bloc was about €95 billion, according to Eurostat and Rhodium Group data.While most legacy Chinese FDI in Europe centered on Germany, France and the Benelux countries, the focus has shifted east in recent years. CEE has attracted more than half of Chinese FDI into the EU and Britain since 2021, according to an analysis by the Rhodium Group, with an even larger regional share when the Western Balkans are included. Hungary has attracted the largest share of new investment since the COVID-19 pandemic, hitting 44% in 2023 and 23% in 2025.The investment surge in CEE has largely been driven by mega-projects in the electric vehicle (EV) supply chain. Chinese EV and battery manufacturers CATL, BYD and Sunwoda are all establishing major Hungarian operations. Slovakia has attracted investment from Chinese battery tech firm Gotion, and will be the site of a new Volvo plant owned by the Chinese automaker Geely.Meanwhile, Serbia, which has significant steel and copper assets, has signed contracts with Chinese auto firms Minth , Shanghai Automotive Chassis (SHAC), BMTS Technology and Xingyu Automotive, envisaging around €1 billion in investment and nearly 1,700 car-parts jobs, according to the government. The deals also include a new robotics factory in Sabac, billed as Europe's first humanoid robot mass production base.These investments can create jobs, spur growth, and accelerate the energy transition, but they may also erode EU competitiveness over time. Outsourcing key advanced manufacturing technologies to Chinese entities risks deepening Europe's dependence on external supply chains and weakening domestic innovation and R&D.DEFEND, THEN COMPETEEurope is seeking to limit China's access to its consumer markets and industries, but the current Franco-German push for faster defensive trade action and tougher investment screening across the bloc appears to be too little too late.Europe's flagship proposal, the Industrial Accelerator Act, leaves manufacturers' key competitiveness gaps unaddressed. Moreover, its screening mechanism would largely leave unexamined Chinese control via ultimate ownership, foreign subsidies and supply-chain concentration - some key issues when looking at CEE's growing dependence.There is also the problem of fragmentation across the bloc. Investment deals might be in one country's interest but could weaken the bloc's collective negotiating position with Beijing. To address this, the continent would likely need a permanent European economic security coordination mechanism to unite trade, competition and national screening authorities that could identify risks before investments become irreversible.Yet the chances of forming such a body at a time of growing political fragmentation within EU countries seem slim.And, ultimately, protectionism can only get Europe so far. It cannot compensate for the region's structural problems, including expensive energy, fragmented capital markets and slow industrial innovation. For that, the region would likely need to create a true energy union and invest in technological innovation. Building trade walls buys time, but not true change.(The views expressed here are those of Martin Vladimirov, director of the Geoeconomics Program of the Center for the Study of Democracy (CSD))

articles.title: Dubai-bound tanker hit in Gulf; Indians injured
articles.summary: A Dubai-bound oil tanker carrying six Indian seafarers was hit by a projectile while transiting the Persian Gulf on Tuesday, leaving four crew members injured, including one Indian national, the government said on Wednesday.Union Minister of Ports, Shipping and Waterways Sarbananda Sonowal identified the vessel as the Liberian-flagged very large crude carrier (VLCC) MT Fujairah Energy, which was travelling from Al Ruwais to Dubai."The remaining 18 crew members, including five other Indian seafarers, are safe and accounted for," Sonowal said on X.— sarbanandsonwal (@sarbanandsonwal) He even added that the government was in contact with the ship management company to ensure medical assistance and the safety of the affected seafarers."We are continuously monitoring the situation and remain in close contact with the ship management company to ensure the ongoing security, medical care and wellbeing of our seafarers," he wrote on X.The incident adds to concerns over the safety of commercial shipping and Indian seafarers in the Persian Gulf and surrounding waters, where vessels have faced repeated attacks.Last month, a Panama-flagged tanker, MT Louise 1, carrying 27 Indian seafarers was hit by limpet mines in the Strait of Hormuz, triggering a fire. The incident occurred 25 nautical miles (46 km) northeast of Oman's Khasab. The government subsequently confirmed that all Indian crew members were safe.Shipping routes, including the Strait of Hormuz, have faced disruptions and attacks since the Iran-US war began in February 2026.According to data from the Washington Institute for Near East Policy, 37 ships were attacked in October, the highest monthly total since the conflict began.
